utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-02-65-PT, the Prosecutor versus Zeljko Mejakic, Momcilo Gruban, Dusan Fustar, and Dusko Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, and Michael McVicker, assisted by Ruth Gustin, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I've just come out another court. Assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCUDDER
utterances.text: I'm Theodore Scudder. I'm here representing Dusan Fustar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slobodanka Nedic, attorney of -- attorney at law from Belgrade, representing Mr. Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUNDJER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Milenko Dundjer, attorney at law, for Momcilo Gruban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Jovan Simic, attorney at law, representing Zeljko Mejakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let me just get it right. It's Mr. Dundjer for Mr. Gruban?

utterances.speaker: MR. DUNDJER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we have a number of matters to get through in this Status Conference. I will proceed according to the list that I have, and I will call on counsel to make comments as appropriate. I'll deal first with the pre-trial motions. There is before the Chamber a motion, a preliminary motion, filed by the Mejakic Defence, and it is awaiting determination by the Trial Chamber. And I have to say that the Chamber will give its decision on this matter soon. There is also a Prosecution motion to amend Schedule B to the indictment. No responses have been received to that motion, and indeed the time for filing such responses has passed. And I am to say again that a decision will be given soon, within a week on this motion. Additional filings following the arrival of Mejakic. At the last conference, the Prosecution had indicated it would need to supplement its pre-trial brief in connection with the criminal responsibility of Mejakic and to add a schedule detailing specific events relating to Mejakic. I required the schedule to be filed by the 20th of August, but on the 21st, the Prosecution filed a notice advising that on further review the schedule was not needed. However, on the 3rd of October, the Prosecution filed a revised consolidated pre-trial brief, which was said to be subject to any further change necessitated by the eventual decision on the Mejakic preliminary motion. In view of the turn of events in this matter, I will require the Prosecution to file a version of the revised pre-trial brief by December -- by Wednesday, 26th November, with the changes identified, with the changes marked, and the Defence teams may supplement their pre-trial briefs in response by Wednesday, 10th December, 2003. I turn next to disclosures. And my information is that considerable efforts have been made with regard to the outstanding matters, in relation to 66(A)(i) and 66(A)(ii) disclosure, and that the only items remaining are an English translation of the statement of Witness number 17 and the disclosure to the Knezevic Defence of some photo boards used for identification. The Fustar and Gruban Defence teams, my information is that they wish to double-check the latest batch of disclosure, so I call on them to give me information on that particular matter. Counsel for Fustar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCUDDER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have just received in Chicago about ten days ago substantial material. I was engaged in a trial at the time. We started to review that material. We have not finished reviewing it. We expect to finish reviewing it shortly, probably within the next ten days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Within the next ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCUDDER
utterances.text: Yes. We also received yesterday two witness statements that we had not received before. I don't believe those relate to Mr. Fustar, but we're looking at those also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I urge you to act very quickly and expeditiously in this matter. Counsel for Gruban.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUNDJER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence team of Momcilo Gruban received yesterday, after the 65 ter meeting, the evidence that we had earlier required under Rule 66(A)(ii), but we will have to review it in the next two days to double-check the material we received yesterday and we'll be ready within two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Within two days. Thank you. Rule 68 disclosure is, I'm told, also largely complete; although, I understand that the matter was complicated by some material from another case, the Kvocka/Omarska case, and the Prosecution had commenced review of this material. Ms. Korner, could you say something about this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. There's been ongoing discussion, if I can put it that way. The Defence -- well, we're going on about 40 CDs of material. Your Honour, disclosure was made in the Omarska appeal. We are now going to review the disclosure that was made in the appeal to see if there's anything which is material Rule 68 in this case, and that will be completed as -- as your senior legal officer was informed, by Christmas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour, I make it absolutely clear, we're fully aware that our obligation under Rule 68 continues throughout, and we keep these matters under review the whole time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I also understand that in order to facilitate this matter, the Mejakic Defence was to meet with the Prosecution to identify particular areas of interest to them which would assist the Prosecution in its searches. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. At yesterday's meeting, the Defence team of Mr. Mejakic suggested - and we believe indeed it would be purposeful - to narrow down our requirements to certain issues and certain subjects which would facilitate the selection of material, and that would also facilitate the search being done by the Prosecution. As soon as we come to Belgrade, we will write this up as soon as we can, and in contact with the Prosecution I think we'll deal with this fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that's very useful. Rule 68 itself is -- is under review, and it may be that your -- the step you're taking is somewhat anticipatory, but it's to be commended. Ms. Korner, Rule 68 material from the Banovic interviews.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's being reviewed effectively as we speak. And we should be able to provide it - I think Ms. Sutherland said - within the next seven days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I turn next to witnesses, dealing first with expert witnesses. The transcripts of Dr. Greve's prior testimony have already been admitted by the Trial Chamber, and therefore she will not be called. And you can confirm this for me, Ms. Korner, but I was just told that in respect of the experts Clark and Wright, that you no longer intend to -- to use them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The evidence that they would have given will effectively be covered by the investigator, Mr. Sebire, who has dealt with all exhumations in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And he will be called as a -- as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he will be called, if required for cross-examination, and I understand it's already been indicated he will be required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And since you're on your feet, I also understand that the -- you do not intend to call any expert in relation to -- to Gruban?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. This was raised yesterday. And we're at a loss to know what your senior legal officer was referring to. Although, we went back and had a look. The only expert, other than Dr. Greve, who you say has been admitted, would be the expert testimony of Dr. Donia in the Brdjanin case, and that will only be called if we cannot reach some kind of agreement on facts which are background matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Rule 92 bis and 89(F). I understand that all the Defence teams have objected to the admission of witness statements under 92 bis unless the witness is called for cross-examination. Much of the evidence is said to go to the acts and conduct of the accused, and therefore not admissible Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. under that Rule. Ms. Korner, I understand that you propose a partial admission of transcripts --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- Of 38 witnesses under 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. Can I explain? All of those 38 witnesses have testified in one trial or another. In order to make this an efficient presentation of the Prosecution case as shortly as possible, we propose to put in the transcripts under Rule 92 bis, excising that part of the transcript that go directly to the acts and conduct of any accused and to call them simply on that short point. We anticipate that with each witness, therefore, evidence in chief should take no more than at a top -- I was going to say top whack -- at a maximum, one hour. So that should narrow things down very much. I know that there's been the ruling by the Appeals Chamber in the Milosevic case on the total admission of all these statements, including those that go to the acts and conduct of the accused, but it's our view we're happy to abide by whatever ruling the Court makes on that, but that the same effect will be achieved by that method, so that the transcripts of the previous testimony go in as the majority of the evidence in chief with a few questions to deal with those matters that go directly to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, I've considered the -- the time. The case is nearly ready for trial, and with that in mind I would require that you file your motion under whatever Rule by November the 26th, and responses from the Defence by December the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're content with that. And we, as I say, we'll excise from that anything that goes directly to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibits. I understand again, Ms. Korner, that you will be filing a motion for leave to add a further 17 exhibits and to withdraw one item?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Did you wish to say anything more in relation to the question of exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think there's one question that is -- but it's tied up with Mr. Simic's representation. And I think it may be as well to discuss that as a -- as a block, because as Your Honour knows, we've got in as an exhibit -- we're proposing to add Prcac's interview. But Your Honour, that's a separate topic on its own, which we do need to place squarely before Your Honour today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But in placing it before me, bear in mind the ruling that the Chamber has already made. I would not wish to have reopened any matter on which the Chamber has already ruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, then can I put it this way: Your Honours have ruled. What we were proposing to do was point out the difficulties that were going to arise, which weren't quite so apparent at the time that we filed our motions. But Mr. Simic has raised that difficulty, which is namely how is he going to represent Mr. Mejakic if Mr. Prcac is a witness or his interview goes in? And the problem equally arises as to how we can have any dealings with Mr. Prcac direct over the question of his testimony when Mr. Simic is acting both for him and for Mejakic. Your Honour, all I can do is -- the matter, I think, was ventilated or attempted to be ventilated before your senior legal officer, and we were told this was a matter for the Trial Chamber. But, Your Honour, I don't -- effectively, we just made our position clear. It is our intention to either call Prcac live as a witness or to put his interview in, if it's accepted. So one way or another, Your Honour, I think that is going to create a problem for -- not for us but certainly for Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let -- let me hear briefly from Mr. Simic. Very briefly, because I think if the Prosecution wants to have this matter settled, if it's a different issue, then they can file a motion. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there is actually no problem here. We are creating one without any reason at all. Namely, this Defence team can immediately accept the admission of the interview of Mr. Prcac and the statement made by Mr. Mejakic before he volunteered to surrender, we also accepted. That is what the Prosecution wants, and we see no other problem here. Another issue, a different issue, is how somebody can call a witness without having any context. He is accused and before the termination of the proceedings against him, he cannot be called here under subpoena. If introducing the interview is a problem, this Defence team is hereby giving its approval immediately. But how can we introduce the interview without any approval? We will not call Mr. Prcac for cross-examination. I believe this resolves all the problems that could possibly arise in this connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. As I said, if the Prosecution is of the view that she has a matter for the consideration of the Chamber, then she can put it to the Chamber. If it is different from the issue that has already been settled -- it may be related, but perhaps different. I turn next to the question of agreed facts. And I understand here that discussions have been going on for some time and agreements have been reached with the individual Defence teams. I'm grateful to the Prosecution for the summary of the status of their discussions that has been submitted. It's -- it's very useful. I note, however, that absent from it is the indication of any agreement from the Mejakic Defence. Does that mean that the Mejakic Defence has not had enough time to -- to come to an agreement on this or -- or that it objects? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have two reasons for not having yet even started to discuss with the Prosecution adjudicated and stipulated facts. The first reason is that we were really hard up for time. We agreed with the Prosecution that within seven or ten days we would make a draft proposal for stipulated facts that we could live with. And the second reason is that the Defence team does not accept any facts from the previous judgement on an Omarska case, and we do not agree with it, even though it's an adjudicated fact. I believe that this proceedings, this case should concentrate on the role of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. What I will do here is, again, bearing in mind the fact that this case is very nearly ready for trial, I will set a date by which the Prosecution is to file a motion for the admission of facts, and that date will take into consideration the fact that Mr. -- the Mejakic Defence needs further time for consideration. So the Prosecution is to file a motion on this matter by December the 17th, and that will give the Mejakic Defence enough time to consult with the Prosecution on this matter, and responses by January the 9th. The length of trial -- I think, Ms. Korner, you had originally indicated six weeks, if there was substantial agreement on the facts of the indictment and the use that could be made of prior testimony under 92 bis or 89(F). If not, then naturally, it would take a much longer time. What is your present estimate?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if we can reach agreement on, as it were, background facts, and, for example, conditions in the camp, and depending on how much cross-examination, obviously, but six weeks seems to me to be utterly realistic estimate for the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If there is agreement on those--

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we can get agreement on the conditions in the camp, which I would have thought were so obvious as to not even be worth arguing about. Then I estimate that six weeks is a reasonable time to finish the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And give another six weeks for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, at this stage I can't assist. I don't know what they intend to do. But, Your Honour, can I emphasise that as far as the Prosecution's concerned we are ready to start trial at any time that the Court orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the intention is to have this trial started at the earliest possible time, early in the new year. Now, once the preliminary motion has been resolved, once the decision has been given, we will fix a date for filing of the Mejakic pre-trial brief and responses, if any, to the revised Prosecution brief. And then I would also set a date for the Pre-Trial Conference. The next Status Conference is to be held by the latest 11th of March next year, and I will set Wednesday, the 10th of March as the date of the next Status Conference. And I understand the next Rule 65 ter Conference has already been scheduled for the 28th of January. Is there any other matter that any counsel wishes to raise before I call on the accused? May I ask the accused, then, whether there is anything which any of them wishes to raise in relation to the case as a whole or in relation to their conditions of detention. I'll start first with Mr. Mejakic. THE ACCUSED MEJAKIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no remarks to make. I have no need to broach any issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fustar? THE ACCUSED FUSTAR: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no remarks to make, no matters to raise. I am satisfied with the Detention Unit, and I have nothing more to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Knezevic? THE ACCUSED KNEZEVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have nothing to say. The conditions in the Detention Unit are good, and I have nothing further to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, on this note of total satisfaction, we adjourn.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
